title.zh: 第一部分 - 安排度假租房

sections.passage:
A woman telephones a holiday rental agency to book a cottage for a family vacation. The agent, Richard, assists her with finding the right property.

The woman explains that she is looking for a cottage for a week's holiday in July for her family, which includes herself, her husband, and their two children aged 8 and 12. They would prefer a coastal location with easy access to the beach. Richard suggests three properties that meet their criteria.

The first option is Seaside Cottage in the village of Thornbury, which is a five-minute walk from the beach. It has three bedrooms, a fully equipped kitchen, a living room with a TV and DVD player, and a small garden. The weekly rental in July is 650 pounds. It has a maximum occupancy of six people and pets are not allowed.

The second option is Harbour View in the town of Westport, which overlooks the harbor and is a ten-minute walk from the sandy beach. It has four bedrooms, two bathrooms, a large kitchen-diner, and a conservatory with sea views. The weekly rate is 850 pounds in July, and it can accommodate up to eight people. Well-behaved dogs are permitted with an additional charge of 25 pounds per pet per week.

The third option is Coastguard Cottage in the village of Pebble Bay, which is directly on the seafront. It has three bedrooms, an open-plan living area, a modern kitchen, and a rooftop terrace. The weekly rental is 750 pounds, with a maximum of five guests. The property has a no-pets policy and no children under five are permitted due to the steep access stairs.

The woman is interested in Harbour View because of the extra bedroom, which would allow the children to have their own rooms. She asks about the deposit and booking process. Richard explains that a 25 percent deposit is required at the time of booking, with the balance due six weeks before arrival. There is also a refundable security deposit of 200 pounds, which is returned within 14 days of departure provided there is no damage.

title.en: Section 2 - Radio Programme About Local Food Markets
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于本地食品市场的广播节目

sections.passage:
Welcome to Local Life, your weekly guide to what's happening in and around the city. I'm Sarah Jenkins, and today I'm talking about the growing trend of local food markets in our region.

Food markets have experienced a remarkable resurgence in recent years. According to the National Market Association, the number of regular food markets in the UK has increased by 35 percent over the past decade, with over 1,200 markets now operating nationwide. This growth reflects a broader shift in consumer attitudes toward locally sourced, artisanal, and organic food.

In our city, we're fortunate to have several excellent markets. The oldest and largest is the Riverside Market, which has been operating every Saturday from 8 AM to 2 PM since 1987. Located on the banks of the River Trent, it features over 60 stalls selling fresh produce, baked goods, cheeses, meats, and ready-to-eat meals. The market has won the Regional Food Market of the Year award three times and attracts approximately 3,000 visitors each week.

The newest addition to our local market scene is the Night Market at the old brewery, which launched last September. This operates on the first Friday of every month from 5 PM to 10 PM and focuses on street food from around the world. You can sample dishes from over 25 different countries, including Thai curries, Mexican tacos, Japanese gyoza, Ethiopian stews, and Brazilian grilled meats. There is also live music, craft beer bars, and cooking demonstrations by local chefs. Admission is free, though some of the premium dining experiences require advance booking.

For those who prefer organic produce, the Green Market operates every Wednesday from 10 AM to 3 PM in the grounds of St. Mary's Church. All vendors must meet strict organic certification standards, and the market also hosts a weekly seed swap where gardeners can exchange seeds and growing tips. There is a popular community cafe run by volunteers that serves seasonal dishes made entirely from market produce.

Finally, for early risers, the Wholesale Farmers Market at the docks opens at 5 AM on weekday mornings. While primarily designed for trade buyers such as restaurants and caterers, it is also open to members of the public who are willing to get up early. Prices are typically 30 to 50 percent lower than retail, and you can buy everything from fresh fish caught that morning to locally grown vegetables and artisan bread.

title.en: Section 3 - Two Students Discussing a Presentation on Urban Planning
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生讨论关于城市规划的演示

sections.passage:
Lisa and Michael are third-year geography students who have been asked to give a joint presentation on sustainable urban planning. They meet in the university cafeteria to discuss their approach.

Lisa has been researching Copenhagen's approach to urban planning, which she believes is one of the best examples of sustainable city design in the world. She explains that Copenhagen has adopted a 'Finger Plan' first developed in 1947, which directs urban development along five corridors radiating from the city center, with green spaces preserved between the fingers. This plan has been remarkably successful in preventing urban sprawl and maintaining accessible green areas for residents.

Michael has been looking at Curitiba in Brazil, a city that has become internationally famous for its innovative public transport system. In the 1970s, under the leadership of Mayor Jaime Lerner, Curitiba introduced a bus rapid transit system that carries over 2.3 million passengers per day. The system uses dedicated bus lanes, elevated tube stations for efficient boarding, and a flat fare structure that encourages usage. The cost of building the system was only 3 percent of what a subway would have cost, making it a model for developing cities worldwide.

They agree to structure their presentation around three main themes: transport, green spaces, and community engagement. For transport, they will compare Copenhagen's cycling infrastructure with Curitiba's bus rapid transit, examining how each city has reduced car dependency. For green spaces, they will discuss Copenhagen's finger plan and Curitiba's network of parks, which was designed to serve a dual purpose: providing recreational space while also functioning as flood management infrastructure along the city's rivers.

Regarding community engagement, Lisa mentions that Copenhagen holds regular public consultations on urban development projects and has a policy of involving residents in the design of local public spaces. Michael adds that Curitiba has implemented an innovative exchange program where residents in low-income areas can exchange recyclable waste for fresh vegetables and bus tokens, combining waste management with food security and public transport access.

They need to submit their presentation slides by next Wednesday and deliver the presentation the following Monday. They agree to divide the work equally, with Lisa taking primary responsibility for the Copenhagen case study and Michael for Curitiba. They plan to meet again on Monday to review each other's sections and ensure a cohesive final product.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the History of Writing Materials
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于书写材料历史的讲座

sections.passage:
Good morning. Today's lecture continues our series on the history of communication technology by examining the development of writing materials from ancient times to the modern era. The ability to record information in written form has been one of the most transformative developments in human civilization, and the materials used for this purpose have evolved dramatically over thousands of years.

The earliest known writing materials were clay tablets, used by the Sumerians of ancient Mesopotamia around 3400 BC. The Sumerians developed a writing system known as cuneiform, which involved pressing a reed stylus into soft clay to create wedge-shaped marks. Once inscribed, the clay tablets were either dried in the sun or fired in a kiln to make them permanent. Thousands of these tablets have survived to the present day, providing invaluable records of ancient Mesopotamian society, including commercial transactions, legal codes, and literary works.

Papyrus, made from the pith of the papyrus plant, emerged as a writing material in ancient Egypt around 3000 BC. The plant, which grows abundantly along the Nile, was cut into strips, soaked, and then layered in two perpendicular directions before being pressed and dried to create a smooth writing surface. Papyrus was lighter and more portable than clay, and it could be rolled into scrolls for easy storage and transportation. It became the dominant writing material throughout the Mediterranean world for nearly 3,000 years.

The invention of parchment, made from animal skins, represented a significant advance. Parchment was more durable than papyrus and could be written on both sides, making it more economical. It was also possible to scrape off the writing and reuse the material, creating what is known as a palimpsest. Parchment was particularly important for the preservation of knowledge during the Middle Ages, when monks in European monasteries spent centuries copying religious texts and classical works onto parchment manuscripts.

Perhaps the most revolutionary development in writing materials was the invention of paper. Paper was first developed in China around 105 AD by Cai Lun, a court official of the Han Dynasty, though recent archaeological discoveries suggest that crude forms of paper existed in China as early as the 2nd century BC. The Chinese manufacturing process involved soaking and pounding plant fibers, primarily from mulberry bark and hemp, into a pulp, then spreading the mixture thinly over a flat screen and allowing it to dry. The technology gradually spread westward along the Silk Road, reaching the Islamic world by the 8th century and Europe by the 12th century.

The mass production of paper was made possible by the invention of the papermaking machine by Louis-Nicolas Robert in France in 1798. This machine could produce continuous rolls of paper, replacing the laborious hand-production method and dramatically reducing the cost. Combined with the development of mechanical printing presses, affordable paper enabled the explosion of literacy and the mass dissemination of information that characterized the 19th and 20th centuries. Today, despite the rise of digital technology, over 400 million tonnes of paper are produced globally each year.

sections.passage:
Our conception of time begins with the revolution of the Earth around the Sun. The length of time the Earth takes to make one complete revolution determines the length of our year, and the time it takes to rotate once on its axis determines the length of our day. But for most of human history, time measurement was far less precise than these astronomical observations might suggest.

The earliest timekeeping devices relied on the movement of the Sun. The sundial, which dates back to at least 3500 BC in ancient Egypt, uses the shadow cast by a gnomon, or pointer, to indicate the time of day. However, sundials are useless at night or on cloudy days, which led to the development of water clocks, or clepsydrae. These devices measured time by the regulated flow of water from one container to another. The oldest known water clock dates from about 1500 BC and was found in the Temple of Amun at Karnak in Egypt.

Mechanical clocks, driven by weights and gears rather than natural forces, first appeared in European monasteries and cathedral towers in the late 13th century. These early clocks were not particularly accurate, often losing or gaining 15 minutes per day. They typically had no dial or hands but struck a bell at regular intervals, which is why we still speak of the clock 'striking' the hour. The word 'clock' itself derives from the Latin 'clocca,' meaning 'bell.'

The development of the pendulum clock by Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens in 1656 marked a quantum leap in accuracy. A pendulum clock could keep time to within a few seconds per day, compared to the 15 minutes per day of earlier mechanical clocks. This improvement was crucial for navigation, as accurate timekeeping was essential for determining longitude at sea. The British government's Longitude Act of 1714 offered a prize of 20,000 pounds, equivalent to several million pounds today, for a practical method of determining longitude within half a degree.

The next major advance came with the development of the marine chronometer by English clockmaker John Harrison in the 1730s. Harrison spent nearly 30 years perfecting his invention, which could keep accurate time aboard a ship despite the motion of the waves and changes in temperature and humidity. His H4 chronometer, completed in 1759, lost only 5 seconds over 81 days during sea trials, far exceeding the accuracy required to win the Longitude Prize. Harrison's achievement was one of the great technological triumphs of the 18th century.

In the 20th century, quartz crystal oscillators and atomic clocks revolutionized timekeeping yet again. The first quartz clock was built in 1927, and quartz watches became widely available in the 1960s. Atomic clocks, which measure the vibrations of cesium atoms, are accurate to within one second in 300 million years and form the basis of the international time standard. GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and use time differences in signals from multiple satellites to determine position on the Earth's surface to within a few meters.

title.en: Passage 2 - Sheet Glass Manufacture: The Float Process
title.zh: 文章2 - 平板玻璃制造：浮法工艺

sections.passage:
Glass, which has been made for over 3,500 years, can be broadly divided into two categories: container glass and flat (or sheet) glass. Flat glass is used primarily in the construction industry for windows and facades, and in the automotive industry for windscreens and windows. The development of the float glass process by Sir Alastair Pilkington in the 1950s revolutionized the production of flat glass and remains the dominant manufacturing method today.

Before the float process, flat glass was produced by several different methods, all of which had significant limitations. The earliest method, known as the crown glass process, involved spinning a blob of molten glass at the end of a rod until it formed a flat disc. The disc was then cut into panes. This process produced glass with good optical clarity but was limited in the size of panes that could be produced and resulted in considerable waste. The plate glass process, developed in the 17th century, involved pouring molten glass onto a flat table, rolling it to an even thickness, and then grinding and polishing both surfaces. While this produced high-quality glass, the grinding and polishing stages were extremely time-consuming and expensive.

The float glass process, which Pilkington developed over seven years at a cost of 7 million pounds, solved these problems elegantly. In the process, a continuous ribbon of molten glass at approximately 1,100 degrees Celsius flows from the melting furnace onto a bath of molten tin. Because the glass is less dense than the tin, it floats on the surface and spreads out to form a perfectly flat sheet. Surface tension ensures that both the top and bottom surfaces are smooth and parallel. The glass then passes through a long annealing chamber, called a lehr, where it is gradually cooled to relieve internal stresses. The entire process from furnace to finished sheet takes approximately 24 hours.

The advantages of the float process over previous methods are numerous. It produces glass of consistent thickness and optical quality, with no need for grinding or polishing. It can produce sheets of virtually any width, limited only by the size of the tin bath. The process is continuous, meaning that production does not need to stop and start as it did with batch methods. Furthermore, the glass produced requires no secondary processing before it can be used, which dramatically reduces manufacturing costs.

Today, over 80 percent of the world's flat glass is produced using the float process, and Pilkington's original patents have long since expired, meaning any manufacturer can use the technology. Modern float glass plants can produce over 1,000 tonnes of glass per day, with sheets ranging in thickness from 0.4 millimeters to 25 millimeters. Recent innovations in the float process include the production of low-emissivity glass, which has a microscopically thin metallic coating that reflects heat while allowing light to pass through, and self-cleaning glass, which has a photocatalytic coating that breaks down dirt when exposed to ultraviolet light.

title.zh: 文章3 - 心灵感应与大脑

sections.passage:
The search for evidence of telepathy, the ability to communicate thoughts directly from one mind to another without using the known senses, has been a focus of parapsychological research for over a century. Despite numerous experiments and claims of success, the scientific community remains deeply divided over whether telepathy is a genuine phenomenon or simply a product of coincidence, wishful thinking, and methodological flaws.

The most famous early telepathy experiments were conducted by J.B. Rhine at Duke University in the United States in the 1930s. Rhine used a set of 25 cards, each bearing one of five symbols: a circle, a square, a star, a cross, or wavy lines. In the standard test, one person, the sender, would look at each card in turn while another person, the receiver, attempted to identify the card purely through mental concentration. With five possible choices, random guessing would produce a correct answer 20 percent of the time. Rhine reported that some subjects consistently scored significantly above this chance level, with certain individuals achieving hit rates of 30 percent or more over thousands of trials.

However, Rhine's work attracted considerable criticism. Skeptics pointed out that the experimental conditions were often inadequate to prevent cheating, that the statistical methods used were sometimes inappropriate, and that many of the most impressive results came from studies that could not be replicated by other researchers. In response to these criticisms, later researchers developed more rigorous experimental protocols, including the use of automated systems to present and record responses, the physical separation of sender and receiver by considerable distances, and the elimination of all possible sensory channels through which information might leak.

One of the most sophisticated modern approaches to testing telepathy uses brain imaging technology. In these experiments, the sender and receiver are placed in separate rooms, and the sender is shown a series of images or video clips while their brain activity is monitored using an electroencephalogram. The receiver, who sees no images, is also monitored for brain activity. Researchers then look for correlations between the brain patterns of the sender and receiver, specifically looking for instances where the receiver's brain responds to the stimulus in a way that mirrors the sender's brain response, even though the receiver has had no sensory exposure to the stimulus.

A team of researchers at the University of Barcelona published results in 2014 claiming to have found evidence of such neural correlations. In their experiment, 15 sender-receiver pairs were tested over multiple sessions. They reported that the receiver's brain showed significant electrical responses that correlated with the sender's exposure to visual stimuli, even though the receivers were in a completely shielded room with no possibility of receiving the information through normal sensory channels. The probability of these results occurring by chance, they claimed, was less than 1 in 10,000.

Despite these intriguing findings, the broader scientific community has not embraced the existence of telepathy. Critics argue that the effect sizes reported are very small, that the results have not been independently replicated with sufficient consistency, and that there is no plausible theoretical mechanism by which thoughts could be transmitted directly between brains. The human brain generates electromagnetic fields, but these are far too weak to be detected at any significant distance by another brain. Until a robust theoretical framework and consistently replicable experimental evidence are provided, telepathy will likely remain on the margins of mainstream science.

text.en: How many sender-receiver pairs were tested in the Barcelona study?
text.zh: 巴塞罗那研究中测试了多少对发送者-接收者？

text.en: What probability of occurring by chance did the Barcelona team claim?
text.zh: 巴塞罗那团队声称的偶然发生的概率是多少？

text.en: What criticism is made of telepathy research findings?
text.zh: 对心灵感应研究结果有什么批评？

options.en: The effect sizes are very large
The effect sizes are very small and results not consistently replicated
options.zh: 效应量非常小且结果未能一致重复

text.en: Why is telepathy considered implausible by critics?
text.zh: 批评者为什么认为心灵感应不可信？

options.en: No one has ever reported experiencing it
Brain electromagnetic fields are too weak to be detected at distance
options.zh: 大脑电磁场太弱，无法在远处被检测到

text.en: Where did J.B. Rhine work?
text.zh: J.B. Rhine在哪里工作？

text.en: How long has parapsychological research on telepathy been conducted?
text.zh: 心灵感应的超心理学研究进行了多长时间？

prompt.en: The pie charts below show the main reasons why agricultural land becomes less productive and the percentage of land degraded in the world's three main regions. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的饼图显示了农业用地生产力下降的主要原因以及世界三个主要地区退化土地的百分比。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关处进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: Some experts believe that it is better for children to begin learning a foreign language at primary school rather than secondary school. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些专家认为，孩子们从小学开始学习外语比从中学开始更好。这样做的优势是否大于劣势？给出你回答的理由，并包括来自你自己的知识或经验的相关例子。至少写250个单词。
